beginner: The Iran war just sent energy prices spiking, and the Fed is worried this could derail the economy. RSM cut their 2026 growth forecast from 2.4% down to 1.7% because the energy shock is real and painful.
Stocks jumped hard on April 8 (Dow up 2.85%, best day since April 2025) because investors got good news about a two-week ceasefire. That relief won't last if energy stays expensive.
The Fed faces an old problem it knows too well: inflation from energy shocks spreads to everything else. Watch whether February's 2.41% inflation print starts creeping higher as pump prices climb.
moderate: The Iran war revived the Fed's nightmare scenario from 2022. Energy costs surge, RSM slashed growth from 2.4% to 1.7%, and the central bank has limited room to cut rates when inflation pressures mount (policy rate sits at 3.64% in February, close to the 3.25% annual forecast).

Stock markets treated the ceasefire as permission to ignore downside risks. The Dow's 2.85% jump on April 8 looks like relief trading, not conviction about economic resilience, especially when GDP growth is already expected to undershoot at 2.2% for the year.

The timing matters. Unemployment at 4.4% and inflation at 2.41% both suggest room for Fed cuts, but energy shocks move faster than monetary policy. If crude stays elevated through Q2, the Fed gets trapped between supporting growth and defending price stability.
expert: RSM downgrade from 2.4% to 1.7% GDP growth reflects a ~70bp energy shock hitting demand and supply simultaneously. February CPI of 2.41% still contained, but lagged pass-through from energy to core inflation typically manifests 6-8 weeks out. Watch April and May prints for confirmation the shock sticks.

Policy rate at 3.64% (February) sits 39bp above the 3.25% full-year forecast, signaling market-implied rate cuts built into the consensus. A sustained energy shock forces the Fed to choose between the 4.2% unemployment forecast and the 2.3% inflation target. Equity relief on the ceasefire (Dow +2.85%) prices in a soft landing the energy data no longer supports.

Forward signal: if energy remains elevated through Q2 earnings season, expect consensus downgrades to accelerate and real yields to reprice higher despite growth concerns. The Fed's next move is reactive, not preventive, and that asymmetry favors volatility in fixed income and equities sensitive to rate path uncertainty.

beginner: Canada's job market is stuck. Unemployment sits at 7% with the forecast expecting only a small drop to 6.7%, meaning the labor market has not recovered the momentum needed to drive growth.
Growth has collapsed to less than 1% annually, which is disastrous for a country that usually grows 2 to 2.5%. Something is broken in the Canadian economy right now, not just soft.

The trade deal renegotiation with the US and Mexico starting next year is a wild card that could upend everything. A weaker negotiating position (slow growth, high unemployment) gives Canada less leverage at the bargaining table.
moderate: Unemployment at 7% tracks well above the 6.5% full-year forecast, and GDP growth below 1% annualized puts Canada in recession territory (two consecutive quarters of negative growth would make it official). The central bank cut rates to 2.25% but demand is not responding.

Canada's labor market weakness mirrors the broader stagnation: companies are not hiring because they lack confidence in future demand. This creates a doom loop where unemployment rises, consumer spending falls, and hiring slows further. Compare this to the US unemployment at 4.4% and you see a two-speed North American recovery.

Trade deal renegotiation in 2025 happens against this economic backdrop. A country with 7% unemployment and sub-1% growth has less room to push back on US demands for tariff concessions or supply chain reshoring. Expect Canada to compromise more than it would in a boom.
expert: Unemployment at 7% (2026-01: 6.74%) versus 6.5% forecast signals the consensus underestimated structural labor market damage. Sub-1% GDP growth annualized, well below the 1.7% full-year forecast, confirms a demand shock not yet reflected in consensus revisions. Policy rate at 2.25% (already at forecast) leaves zero more easing room.

CPI at 1.78% (February, lowest among peer G7) provides cover for further BoC cuts, but rate cuts without demand recovery just compress net interest margins on bank balance sheets and deepen deflation risk. The 2% inflation forecast assumes a demand rebound that recent data does not support.

Forward: USMCA renegotiation in 2025 occurs in a Canadian economy showing near-zero growth momentum. Equity underperformance and currency weakness versus USD create a political economy where deeper trade concessions become likely. Watch for sectoral squeeze in autos and agriculture first.

beginner: BlackRock is betting that the UK is undervalued and has positioned to go long UK Gilts while shorting other European bonds. Big money is starting to see the UK as the better deal right now.
The government plans to tighten the budget after 2026, which means austerity is coming. This could slow growth but might actually attract investors who want fiscal discipline and stable gilt yields.

Inflation at 3.24% is still above target, which keeps the Bank of England from cutting rates aggressively even though growth is weak at 1.5% forecast. The UK is caught between sticky prices and sluggish demand.
moderate: BlackRock's long UK Gilts, short German Bunds positioning reflects a view that UK fiscal consolidation (expected in 2027 after a neutral 2025-2026) will deliver credible disinflation, while German fiscal drag is already priced in. The UK offer relative value versus crowded shorts elsewhere in Europe.

CPI at 3.24% (February) sits above the 2.5% forecast, forcing the BoE to hold rates at 3.75% even as growth tracks below expectations at 1.5%. The central bank has less room to support demand without losing inflation credibility, making near-term gilt volatility a feature, not a bug.

The OECD assumes sizable fiscal consolidation in 2027 after neutral fiscal stances in 2025 and 2026. This timeline creates a window: gilts rally into 2026 on the expectation of future discipline, but growth likely deteriorates in 2027 when austerity hits. Position accordingly.
expert: CPI at 3.24% (February) versus 2.5% full-year forecast signals sticky services inflation and persistent wage pressures. BoE policy rate at 3.75% (against 3.25% forecast) means terminal rate has shifted higher. Gilt curve is pricing multiple hold cycles, not cuts, through mid-2026.

BlackRock's long GBP Gilts versus short German Bunds reflects a technical arbitrage on fiscal credibility. UK fiscal consolidation expected 2027 (OECD assumption) creates a 12-month window where gilts outperform on future tightening expectations. German bunds suffer crowded positioning and negative carry.

Forward signal: the UK labor market (unemployment 5.2% November, lagged data) and wage growth dynamics will determine if BoE holds or cuts into 2027. A miss on disinflation forces the BoE to extend holds, which would break the BlackRock thesis and reprice gilts lower. Watch Q1-Q2 wage data releases carefully.

beginner: Japan is on the verge of losing its position as the third-largest economy in the world. India is about to overtake Japan in 2026, which is a humbling milestone for a wealthy nation.

Japan's growth rate is the lowest in the major economies, and here is the stunning part: Japanese GDP per capita has actually declined over the past 25 years. The country is not just growing slowly, it is shrinking in real per-person terms.

With inflation at just 1.26% and unemployment at 2.4%, Japan looks stable on the surface. But those numbers mask a deeper problem: a population that is not spending, not borrowing, and not taking risks. The policy rate at 0.75% shows the central bank still has room to act, but stimulus cannot fix demographic decline.
moderate: India is set to overtake Japan as the 4th largest economy in 2026 (Germany already took 3rd in 2023), a symbolic end to Japan's postwar dominance. This reflects not a Japanese collapse but a structural lag: Japan's growth forecast of 0.8% is half Canada's 1.7% and one-quarter the US forecast of 2.2%.

GDP per capita declined over 25 years despite price stability and low unemployment. This inversion (strong labor market, weak per-capita income) signals that wage growth has lagged productivity gains, or more likely, that deflation-fighting stimulus created asset inflation while real wages stagnated. The BoJ raised rates to 0.75% despite this backdrop, signaling confidence in the recovery.

Demographic headwinds are structural, not cyclical. Japan's current account surplus of 4.8% (forecast) versus negative balances elsewhere shows the nation is a net saver and exporter, not a consumer. Rate hikes will likely persist because inflation expectations are finally shifting, but growth will remain a structural drag.
expert: Japan's 0.8% 2026 growth forecast is the lowest in the G7. CPI at 1.26% (February) and policy rate at 0.75% (February) show the BoJ is hiking despite sub-1% growth, betting on wage and expectations anchoring. The 1.25% full-year forecast rate implies 50bp more tightening, aggressive by historical standards for a 0.8% growth regime.

Per-capita GDP decline over 25 years with current account surplus of 4.8% reveals a dual pathology: household real income weakness despite labor market strength (2.4% unemployment) and persistent corporate sector cash hoarding. The BoJ's rate path assumes domestic demand reaccelerates, a forecast signal unsupported by recent household spending data.

Forward: India overtaking Japan as 4th largest economy in 2026 is demographically inevitable but marks the moment when BoJ policy tightening becomes growth-negative rather than structural. Watch Q2-Q3 wage data for evidence of sustained inflation, and household consumption surveys for signs of demand destruction from rate hikes. A growth miss forces policy reversal by late 2026.

beginner: Germany's economy barely moved in early 2026, with inflation stuck near 2% and unemployment holding steady at 3.6%. The real story is whether the government can unblock growth by fixing red tape and energy costs, because 1.2% annual growth is anaemic for Europe's biggest economy.

BlackRock is betting against German stocks right now, sensing the rally at the start of the year was overdone. When the world's largest asset manager is shorting your market, it signals serious doubts about the recovery story.

The ECB cut rates to 2.15% in March, but that won't matter if Germany's problems are structural (bureaucracy, energy prices) rather than cyclical (too much demand). Watch whether the government actually delivers on promised reforms.
moderate: Germany's CPI at 1.9% in February puts it below the ECB's 2.15% policy rate in real terms, yet growth forecasts sit at just 1.2% for 2026. Compare this to Germany's pre-pandemic trend of 1.5% to 2% growth: even with easier monetary policy, the economy is underperforming its historical norm, suggesting demand destruction runs deeper than rate cuts can fix.

The 3.6% unemployment rate masks a labour market increasingly squeezed by structural rigidity. Germany's fiscal deficit sits at 2% of GDP despite weak growth, leaving little room for stimulus if the slowdown accelerates through 2026.

BlackRock's short positions reflect a crowded market trade reversing. Institutional flows matter more than central bank signals when momentum shifts, and the 'German Fiscal Emergence' volatility in early 2026 suggests positioning has become fragile.
expert: CPI 1.9% (February) tracking 40bps below the 2.3% 2026 forecast midpoint, with the ECB at 2.15% in March, creates negative real rates but insufficient to overcome the structural headwinds. Unemployment at 3.6% is near NAIRU, constraining wage flexibility and limiting the Phillips curve transmission mechanism.

Budget deficit at 2% GDP in a 1.2% growth environment signals fiscal constraints ahead. OECD consolidation assumptions post-2026 imply either growth acceleration or political willingness to cut spending, neither of which recent data supports.

Watch the current account surplus (4.5% GDP forecast): if export weakness in autos and industrial goods persists through Q2 2026, external demand may become the binding constraint on growth, requiring either euro depreciation or domestic demand stimulus that the fiscal path doesn't allow.

beginner: France is stuck in slow motion with inflation nearly gone (0.9% in February) while unemployment holds at 7.7%, nearly double Germany's rate. Growth at 0.7% in 2025 slowed to a crawl, and the recovery to 0.9% in 2026 looks fragile at best.
The government is facing massive fiscal consolidation after 2026, which means austerity is coming. That's a headwind for growth when the economy is already limping along.

France's labour market is the real problem. High structural unemployment despite ECB rate cuts suggests the issue is skills, regulation, or wage rigidity, not demand. A tighter fiscal policy makes that worse, not better.
moderate: France's 0.9% CPI print in February is the lowest across the eurozone, reflecting both demand weakness and energy price softness. The 7.7% unemployment rate is more than double Germany's and hasn't budged in a year, signalling a labour market trapped in low-productivity equilibrium rather than temporarily slack.

The Banque de France expects 0.9% growth in 2026 after 0.7% in 2025, a marginal improvement that barely exceeds the eurozone's long-term potential. Compare this to Spain's resilience (above 2% growth): France's economy lacks the flexibility to adapt to post-pandemic demand shifts.

OECD consolidation assumptions kick in hard after 2026, implying 1.5% to 2% of GDP in fiscal drag. With growth forecast at only 0.9%, that ratio of adjustment to growth is historically contractionary, likely dragging unemployment higher.
expert: CPI at 0.9% (February) tracks 110bps below the 2% 2026 forecast, with policy rate at 2.15% delivering substantially positive real rates. This deflation bias persists despite ECB accommodation, pointing to demand destruction rather than temporary supply shock.

Unemployment at 7.7% with growth forecast at 1.4% for the full year implies NAIRU well above 6%, making labour market slack structural rather than cyclical. Wage growth will remain compressed, limiting demand recovery even as monetary conditions ease.

The OECD's fiscal consolidation assumption for 2027 creates a cliff: if 2026 growth underperforms the 0.9% forecast (high probability given current momentum), the multiplier on subsequent consolidation swings from 0.5 to 1.2x, risking a 2027 recession.

beginner: Italy's exports are cratering, especially to the United States, because of the trade war and global tension. Growth barely happened in 2025 and the 2026 forecast of 1% is weak for any developed economy.
Inflation at 1.51% is tame, but unemployment sits at 5.6% and the government must tighten the budget after 2026. That means less government support just when the economy needs help.
Italy's economy is increasingly dependent on eurozone stability and EU funding. When trade turns ugly (and it has), Italy has fewer levers to pull than larger peers.
moderate: Italian goods exports outside the euro area contracted sharply in 2025, with US shipments hit hardest as tariffs bit. CPI at 1.51% in February reflects this demand shock, not price stability, and the 1% growth forecast assumes the trade war doesn't worsen.

Unemployment at 5.6% is lower than France's but still elevated relative to Germany's 3.6%, and the labour market lacks the dynamism to absorb more shocks. Regional unemployment in the South remains above 10%, creating political pressure to avoid fiscal cuts.

OECD consolidation in 2027 coincides with what may be a second wave of trade tension. Italy's 0.8% current account surplus offers some buffer, but the economy cannot simultaneously deliver deficit reduction and growth acceleration if external demand deteriorates.
expert: CPI at 1.51% (February) reflects demand destruction from trade shock, not price anchoring. Policy rate at 2.15% creates positive real rates in a 1% growth environment, effectively tightening conditions when the economy needs relief.

Export contraction (denominated in dollars and euros) signals competitiveness pressure within the eurozone. Italy cannot depreciate, wage deflation is slow, and productivity gains are modest, leaving limited margin for absorption of tariff shocks without volume losses.

The OECD consolidation trigger (2027) hits as trade tensions may have persisted 12+ months, creating a policy trilemma: fiscal rules require consolidation, external demand remains weak, and monetary policy is constrained by eurozone inflation risks. Watch Q2 2026 PMI for early signal of whether the demand shock is temporary or structural.

beginner: US-China trade collapsed by $170 billion in 2025, roughly a quarter of the total bilateral flow. China's economy is slowing and needs fiscal stimulus to hit the 4.5% growth target for 2026.

Inflation in China is near zero (0.23% in January), giving the government room to spend without stoking prices. The question is whether stimulus will actually reach consumers or just prop up old industries.

A stronger yuan would normally be good news for savers, but it tightens monetary conditions when China's growth is already soft. The government faces a trade-off between currency strength and growth support.
moderate: Trade volumes fell by one quarter in 2025, a shock magnitude unseen since the 2008 crisis. China's 4.5% growth forecast requires 'more expansionary fiscal policy,' but Chinese stimulus has shown declining effectiveness (2015-2020 multipliers halved relative to 2008-2010). The question is not whether Beijing will spend, but whether it works.

CPI at 0.23% in January is deflationary and gives policymakers cover, but it also signals weak demand domesticity (not just external trade shock). Unemployment at 4.9% is officially stable but provincial youth unemployment tells a different story.

The renminbi strength assumption in the forecast contradicts the growth path: a stronger currency tightens financial conditions at the moment China needs accommodation. If the dollar weakens as assumed, capital outflow pressures may force Beijing to choose between currency support and monetary easing.
expert: Trade contraction of $170 billion represents 23% of 2024 flows, concentrated in electronics and industrial goods. China's 4.5% growth forecast assumes fiscal multiplier of 1.1x at minimum, but recent stimulus (2023-2025) yielded multiplier closer to 0.6x, implying actual trajectory closer to 3.5% unless structural constraints ease.

CPI at 0.23% (January) with unemployment at 4.9% creates a Phillips curve mystery: slack exists but wage growth remains subdued, pointing to labour market segmentation and productivity deflation in low-margin sectors. Policy rate (forecast 2.75%) sits well above inflation, in real tightening territory.

Renminbi appreciation in a weaker-dollar scenario creates policy bind: tighter financial conditions via currency channel when fiscal stimulus is needed to offset trade shock. Watch March-April credit growth and July 2026 labour market data for signal of whether fiscal thrust actually reaches real economy or stalls in property/SOE balance sheets.

beginner: India's economy is firing on all cylinders. Growth hit 8% in the first half of the fiscal year, which is exactly what you want to see when most of the world is slowing down.
The country just overtook Japan to become the world's 4th largest economy. That's not a ranking quirk, it's a sign that India's domestic consumption and manufacturing are reshaping global economics.
Inflation sits at a sleepy 1.33%, giving policymakers room to keep supporting growth without overheating the economy. The central bank has space to cut rates if needed.
moderate: India's 8% growth in the first half of FY2026 is running well ahead of the full-year 6.3% forecast, signaling domestic demand remains robust even as global growth wobbles. Infrastructure spending and manufacturing gains are the twin engines.
Surpassing Japan to rank 4th globally reflects a structural shift, not a temporary rebound. India's working-age population and consumer base dwarf Japan's, and that gap will only widen.
December CPI of 1.33% sits far below the 4.2% full-year forecast, giving the central bank flexibility. The policy rate at 5.25% can afford to move lower if growth momentum cools.
expert: Real GDP growth of 8% in H1 FY2026 tracks materially above the 6.3% full-year consensus, driven by sustained domestic demand and capex cycles that show no sign of faltering. Watch for any moderation in quarterly prints as base effects normalize.

India's PPP-adjusted economy now ranks 4th globally at roughly $14-15 trillion, ahead of Japan's $6-7 trillion nominal base. This reflects genuine structural economic power, not currency distortion, and signals enduring competitive advantage in labor-intensive manufacturing.

The 5.25% policy rate with inflation at 1.33% implies real rates around 3.9%, still restrictive. Forward guidance and the next RBI decision will signal whether the central bank pivots to accommodation as full-year growth may undershoot Q1-Q2 momentum.

beginner: South Africa's unemployment rate sits at a crushing 31.88%, the worst jobs crisis among major emerging markets. That's not a headline, that's an economic emergency.

The central bank holds the policy rate at 6.75%, one of the lowest levels in years, trying to stimulate hiring. But cheap money can't fix structural problems like lack of skills and crumbling infrastructure.
South Africa ranks among Africa's three largest economies but that status masks a reality: growth is projected at just 1.5% for the year, and without job creation, political instability could worsen.
moderate: At 31.88%, South Africa's unemployment rate exceeds even the worst readings from the 2008 financial crisis. This is a multi-decade structural failure, not a cyclical downturn, driven by skills gaps, labor rigidity, and inadequate infrastructure investment.

The central bank cut rates to 6.75% as part of a broader emerging market pivot toward accommodation, betting that lower borrowing costs will unlock private investment and job creation. That bet is not paying off yet.

February CPI at 2.96% is well below the 3.5% full-year forecast, giving policymakers cover for further easing. But rate cuts alone cannot address the supply-side constraints and policy dysfunction that plague job creation.
expert: The 31.88% unemployment rate in December 2025 persists despite a 6.75% policy rate, the lowest in the current cycle, signaling that monetary accommodation alone cannot reverse labor market dysfunction. Youth unemployment and skills mismatch dominate the problem.

February CPI printed 2.96% versus a 3.5% full-year forecast, with core inflation moderating. This suggests the central bank has room for 75-100 basis points of further cuts if growth deteriorates, though transmission to employment remains unproven.

Forward expectations: The 1.5% full-year growth forecast assumes no major policy shocks, but given current unemployment trends and weak capex, watch for downside revisions. Political instability could force the central bank to defend the currency at the expense of further rate cuts.

beginner: Brazil's central bank jacked the policy rate to 15% and inflation is still climbing at 3.81%. This is a country that got too hot and now has to pump the brakes hard.

Growth is slowing from 2.4% last year to a projected 1.7% this year as higher rates kill investment and borrowing. The central bank chose inflation control over growth, which is painful but necessary.
BlackRock is betting against Brazil and other high-flying emerging markets. That's a signal that the easy money phase is over and investors are rotating out.
moderate: Brazil's 15% policy rate in February reflects aggressive tightening to corral inflation, yet February CPI still sits at 3.81% versus a 4.2% full-year forecast. The lag between rate hikes and inflation response is stretching longer than expected, raising questions about transmission.

Growth is decelerating from 2.4% in 2025 to a projected 1.7% in 2026 as investment slows in response to elevated borrowing costs. The central bank is accepting near-zero real growth to break inflation expectations.

BlackRock's tactical short on Brazil signals that sophisticated investors are skeptical the central bank can engineer a soft landing. Currency depreciation and capital outflows could force further rate increases, creating a negative feedback loop.
expert: The 15% policy rate as of February 2026 reflects a cumulative tightening cycle that has yet to fully cool inflation, which printed 3.81% in February against a 4.2% full-year forecast. Real rates (nominal minus expected inflation) are now deeply restrictive at roughly 11-12%, signaling the central bank has moved past neutral.

Growth is decelerating from 2.4% in 2025 to a 1.7% full-year forecast, a path consistent with the central bank's inflation mandate but creating structural headwinds for capex and employment. The unemployment rate at 5.8% in February remains benign, but watch for upward pressure as the tightening cycle propagates through demand.

Forward signal: The central bank's forward guidance suggests easing begins in 2026 only if inflation stabilizes. Given currency weakness and external vulnerabilities, any easing cycle is likely to be slow and conditional, keeping real rates elevated through mid-year and capping near-term growth.

beginner: Russia's economy is worth $7.3 trillion when you adjust for what money actually buys in each country. That makes it Europe's largest economy and the 4th biggest in the world, a stunning turnaround from years of stagnation.
GDP per capita jumped 811% since 2000, a massive gain driven by oil production ramping back up after decades of decline. That's real wealth creation, not just ruble devaluation.

The policy rate sits at 15.5% and inflation at 6.01%, meaning the central bank is fighting to keep prices under control while the economy runs hot. High rates usually kill growth, but Russia's oil wealth is cushioning the blow.
moderate: Russia's PPP-adjusted economy ranks 4th globally at $7.3 trillion, a structural gain reflecting decades of underutilization of energy assets and human capital finally being deployed. This is not a sanctions-driven illusion but a genuine shift in global economic geography.

GDP per capita growth of 811% since 2000 outpaces every other major emerging market and reflects both oil price cycles and production expansions. The current tightening cycle at 15.5% policy rate will test whether growth can persist as real rates turn restrictive.

January CPI at 6.01% with unemployment at a taut 2.15% signals an economy running near full capacity. The central bank faces a classic Phillips curve trade-off: rates must stay elevated to prevent wage-driven inflation, constraining near-term output growth.
expert: Russia's purchasing-power-adjusted GDP of $7.3 trillion and 4th-place global ranking reflects structural energy production gains and currency depreciation working in tandem. This is not consensus economics and implies significant geopolitical asymmetry in the event of any sanctions relief.

The 15.5% policy rate in February 2026 with 6.01% CPI and 2.15% unemployment signals an economy operating above potential output. Real rates (nominal minus expected inflation) are roughly 9-10%, restrictive enough to slow capex but not so severe as to create slack, given energy export revenues.

Forward implication: The 1.2% full-year growth forecast assumes no material change in sanctions regimes or oil price shocks. Watch for any moderation in core inflation as a signal that the central bank can pivot toward easing in Q3-Q4 2026, which would unlock capex-driven upside surprises.

beginner.label: America and Iran Stop Fighting

Iran said it will reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz shipping route where much of the world's oil flows
Both sides will meet in Pakistan on Saturday to try negotiating a permanent peace deal

beginner.label: Stock Markets Jump Worldwide
bullets: The S&P 500 rose 2.5% as investors felt relieved that the war might end soon
Oil prices crashed from above $110 to around $94 per barrel on the news
Technology companies and airlines saw their stock prices rise the most

beginner.label: Peace Deal Still Fragile
bullets: Israel kept attacking Lebanon even after the ceasefire, making Iran angry again
Only two ships have actually passed through the Strait of Hormuz so far despite promises
The two-week truce could collapse if either side breaks their promises

moderate.label: America and Iran Stop Fighting
bullets: Trump backed down from his 8 PM deadline threat after Pakistan's leader asked for more time to negotiate
The ceasefire depends on Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, which carries 20% of global oil supplies
This ends six weeks of fighting that began when the conflict spread beyond the original war zone

moderate.label: Stock Markets Jump Worldwide
bullets: The relief rally pushed the S&P 500 above its 200-day moving average for the first time in weeks
Energy stocks like Exxon and Chevron fell as oil prices tumbled 15% in a single day
Tech companies gained on hopes that supply chain disruptions would ease quickly

moderate.label: Peace Deal Still Fragile
bullets: Israeli strikes on Lebanon hours after the deal raised questions about whether the truce covers all fronts
Shipping executives say they still don't know how to safely transit through Iranian-controlled waters
Markets could reverse quickly if the Strait of Hormuz closes again before talks conclude

expert.label: America and Iran Stop Fighting
bullets: Trump accepted Iran's 10-point proposal 90 minutes before his infrastructure bombing deadline, signaling tactical retreat from maximum pressure
The deal requires coordinated transit through Hormuz with Iranian forces, giving Tehran effective control over the chokepoint
Saturday's Islamabad talks with VP Vance leading the US team will determine if this becomes a 45-day framework

bullets: The S&P 500's 2.5% surge to 6,783 broke above the 200-day MA at 6,655, with VIX collapsing to 20 from elevated levels
WTI crude's 15% plunge from $112 to $94 unwound the geopolitical risk premium but futures markets price normalization by H2
Energy sector underperformance versus 6.5% Meta gains signals rotation back to growth names on supply chain relief

expert.label: Peace Deal Still Fragile

Only bulk carriers, not oil tankers, have transited the strait as coordination protocols remain unclear to commercial operators
Any resumption of hostilities before April 22 would validate Goldman's 5,400 S&P 500 bear case on persistent energy shock
